Test "Consumer Purchase Intent Survey for Home Body-Fat Analyser" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey of Japanese adults (aged 18-65) who report owning a bathroom scale and being interested in health monitoring. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two price points: a premium price (e.g., ¥15,000) and a lower price (e.g., ¥12,000). They are asked: "Would you purchase a home body-fat analyser that uses bioelectrical impedance and costs [price] within the next 6 months?" (Yes/No).. Sample: 500 respondents (250 per price group) recruited via an online panel representing Japanese households with bathroom scales.. Measure: Purchase intent (Yes) for each price point.. Predictions: T1: At least 55% of respondents in the premium group will indicate intent, while intent in the lower group will be ≤45%.; T2: At least 50% of respondents in both price groups will indicate intent, with the lower price group showing ≥10% higher intent than the premium group.. Decision rule: If the premium group intent ≥55% and lower group intent ≤45%, proceed with premium-focused launch (supports T1). If both groups intent ≥50% and lower group intent ≥10% higher, proceed with lower-price launch (supports T2). If neither condition is met, abandon launch.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

sources.excerpt: An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere’s Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.
Deere had purchased several competitive lawn and garden tractors to make evaluations on pros and cons of each brand.
International Harvester introduced the Cub Cadet in 1961; Wheel Horse, Bolens, and Simplicity, to mention a few, were also dominate players before John Deere came onto the scene.
Production of the company’s first lawn and garden tractor began at Horicon in 1963, when John Deere built 1000 units of the 110 model.

Test "Japanese Household Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with two randomized groups. Group A sees a product description emphasizing home use for health tracking (body composition monitoring). Group B sees a product description emphasizing home use for fitness tracking (tracking progress after gym sessions). Both groups are recruited from a panel of Japanese adults aged 25-55 who report regular gym attendance or home exercise. Participants are asked: "Would you purchase a stand-on body-fat analyser for home use within the next 12 weeks?" (Yes/No).. Sample: 200 respondents (100 per group). Sample size chosen to detect a 10% difference in purchase intent with 80% power at 5% significance, assuming 20% baseline intent.. Measure: Purchase intent (Yes) and purchase intent score (1=Definitely Yes, 2=Maybe Yes, 3=Maybe No, 4=Definitely No). Secondary measure: stated primary reason for purchase (health tracking vs fitness tracking).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show ≥15% higher purchase intent than Group B because health-conscious households drive demand.; T2: Group B will show ≥15% higher purchase intent than Group A because fitness-oriented consumers drive demand.. Decision rule: If Group A purchase intent ≥ Group B +10%, proceed with home health focus (supports T1). If Group B purchase intent ≥ Group A +10%, proceed with home fitness focus (supports T2). If difference <10%, inconclusive and recommend no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.
